notes.short: “Land, land, land”: one call said three times
notes.about: The prophet calls on the land three times in a row. The repetition gives the call its weight and draws close attention to the solemn and certain word that follows about Coniah and his line (verse 30). It can also be read as hammer blows on a people hardened against God's warnings.

figure.name: Epizeuxis
figure.means: a call made three times, to give it weight and make the land heed the solemn word that follows

original.note: In Hebrew the word said three times is erets, which can mean land or earth.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Epizeuxis, a word repeated to mark it and draw attention. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the triple summons gives it special emphasis and marks what follows as weighty. Benson: the word is repeated for emphasis and deeper attention. Plumptre (Ellicott): the solemn repetition shows the decree is certain. Calvin likens it to hammer strokes on hardened hearts.

cites.quote: It is a common and powerful way of emphasizing a particular word, by thus marking it and calling attention to it.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The land is to take the king's fate sore to heart. The triple repetition of the summons: Land, gives it a special emphasis, and marks the following sentence as of high importance
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: the repetition was not superfluous in exclaiming “earth” three times, for as the hardness of iron is overcome by the repeated strokes of the hammer, so the Prophet repeated the word “earth,” that he might subdue that perverseness in which the Jews had so hardened themselves that no threats of God moved them.
The word earth, or land rather, as ארצ may be properly rendered, is repeated three times by way of emphasis, to engage the deeper attention.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: The solemnity of the mystic threefold repetition expresses the certainty of the Divine decree

notes.short: A question that answers itself: they cannot change
notes.about: The LORD asks a question with only one answer. An Ethiopian cannot change his skin, nor a leopard its spots, and Judah, long trained in evil, can no more turn and do good by itself. Doing evil had become as fixed in them as the color of a skin.

figure.name: Erotesis
figure.words: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?
figure.means: those long used to doing evil can no more turn and do good than a skin or spots can change

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Erotesis, questions about what cannot be. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says the question denies the very thing it raises, so the one is as impossible as the other. Henry, Calvin and Plumptre (Ellicott) say Judah's evil had grown too fixed for it to reform. Clarke agrees the skin cannot change but reads the moral point as extreme difficulty.
notes.limit: Most take the change as impossible for Judah; one reads it as extremely hard and seldom seen. Some add that God's grace can do what man cannot, and verse 27 still pleads with Jerusalem to be made clean. The verse speaks of people trained in evil by long practice.

cites.at: Erotesis, in Absurdities and Impossibilities, p. 956
cites.quote: “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? then may ye also do good, that are accustomed to do evil” (Jer 13:23 ). See Parœmia .
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The consequential clause introduced by גּם אתּם connects with the possibility suggested in, but denied by, the preceding question: if that could happen, then might even ye do good. The one thing is as impossible as the other.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, that is by nature black, or the leopard his spots, that are even woven into the skin? Dirt contracted may be washed off, but we cannot alter the natural colour of a hair ... much less of the skin; and so impossible is it, morally impossible, to reclaim and reform these people.

God declares in this verse, that the people were so hardened in their wickedness, that there was no hope of their repentance. ... he says that they could not repent, that wickedness had become inherent, or firmly fixed in their hearts, like the blackness which is inherent in the skin of the Ethiopians
The meaning of the question is obvious. The evil of Judah was too deep-ingrained to be capable of spontaneous reformation.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: These things are natural to them, and they cannot be altered; so sin, and especially your attachment to idolatry, is become a second nature ... But the expression does not imply that the thing is as impossible in a moral as it is in a natural sense: it only shows that it is extremely difficult, and not to be often expected

notes.short: A saying: can the leopard change his spots?
notes.about: The verse asks two questions whose plain answer is no: can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots? It then applies them: those accustomed to doing evil are not able to do good. The questions are read as a saying first found here that has since passed into common use.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?
figure.means: as the Ethiopian cannot change his skin nor the leopard his spots, so those accustomed to doing evil are not able to do good

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the two questions under Parœmia, among sayings first found in Scripture that have since passed into general use as proverbs. The verse itself applies them to those accustomed to doing evil.
notes.limit: The verse itself does not call the questions a proverb; they count as one because the saying has since passed into common use.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 763
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture; but, which, owing to their fulness of meaning and their wide application, have since passed into general use as proverbial sayings ... “Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?”

notes.short: Cursed and like a shrub; blessed and like a tree
notes.about: A curse on the man who trusts in mankind is followed by a picture of him, a shrub in the desert. A blessing on the man who trusts in the LORD is followed by its picture, a tree planted by the waters.

lines.words: Cursed is the man who trusts in mankind,
He will be like a shrub in the desert;
But blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD,
He is like a tree planted by the waters

notes.evidence: Boys sets the four verses out in four members that take turns: a curse and a blessing in the first and third, and a confirmation or reason for each in the second and fourth.

cites.quote: Here we have a curse and a blessing in A. and A.; and a confirmation, or reason for each, in B. and B. … The leading terms very distinctly mark out for us the arrangement of the passage.

notes.short: A saying: what is straw compared to grain?
notes.about: The LORD has spoken of prophets who prophesy lies in His name, saying, “I had a dream!” (verse 25). Let the dreamer retell his dream, He says, and the one with His word speak it truthfully. Then He asks a question that later became a common saying: “For what is straw compared to grain?”

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: what is straw compared to grain
figure.means: a saying that straw is nothing beside grain; the verse sets the prophet's dream beside the LORD's word

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the question under Parœmia, among proverbs that first appear in Scripture and have since come into common use as sayings. The verses around it (23:25-27 and 32) tell of prophets who prophesy lies and false dreams in the LORD's name, and the verse sets their dreams beside His word.
notes.limit: The verse does not call the question a saying; it is counted one because it later came into common use.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 763
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture; but, which, owing to their fulness of meaning and their wide application, have since passed into general use as proverbial sayings ... “What is the chaff (Heb., straw) to the wheat?”

notes.short: A saying that blamed the fathers for the children
notes.about: People said that the fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth were set on edge, meaning they suffered for their fathers' sins, not their own. It can be read as a charge that God was unjust. The LORD says it will be said no more: instead, “each will die for his own iniquity” (verse 30).

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Quoted as being already in use as such
figure.words: The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge
figure.means: the children are punished for their fathers' sins, not for their own

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists it under Parœmia, a proverb already in use, and points to Ezekiel 18:2-3. Calvin says the people used it to strive with God, as if He punished them while innocent; Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) reads it as a complaint that God is unjust. Plumptre (Ellicott) says it was in common use and eased their consciences; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the exiles' children used it.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which are quoted as being already in use as such, p. 757
cites.quote: “In those days they shall say no more, ‘The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.’ ” This is what they did once say. See Eze 18:2-3.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Ezekiel shews that it was a complaint commonly prevailing among the people, that they suffered for the sins of their fathers ... Such, then, was the arrogance of the Jews, as to strive with God, as though he punished them, while they were innocent; and they expressed this by using a proverb

The proverb means, "Children atone for the misdeeds of their fathers," or "The sins of the fathers are visited on their innocent children." ... The proverb mentioned in Jer 31:29 involves the complaint against God, that in punishing sin He deals unjustly.
